01
Overview

One counter, three real businesses

Before the storefront existed, VS Veronixx was already a shop selling stationery and electrical goods, plus a legal consultancy run by one of the two owners. The digital product had to represent all of that honestly.

The pamphlet printed for the shop counter lists Stationery, Electrical & Electronics and Legal Consultancy side by side, under Rajendra Singh (M.Sc Mathematics) and Vishal Sisodhiya (B.E. EEE, MBA Ops, Advocate). That structure — one shop, several trades — is the reason the product isn't a single "online store" template: it's three connected systems built for one physical counter.

1 · Customer storefront

Browse categories, add to cart, check out as a pickup or delivery request — settlement happens at the counter, not online.

2 · POS terminal

"VS Veronixx Retail OS" — a passcode-locked register for billing, GST, inventory, purchase orders and receipts.

3 · Veronica, AI concierge

A chat widget that searches the catalogue and drafts an order request. She can suggest; only the POS can sell.

What each surface is for

Boundary Per the project's own production baseline: live inventory sync, POS synchronisation and an online payment gateway are all explicitly not connected — by design, not by omission. The storefront runs on a verified static catalogue; floor stock is confirmed over WhatsApp.

02
Problem & goals

Give a working shop a digital counter it can trust

Before any screen was drawn, the brief was reduced to one problem statement, three questions and four principles. Every later decision passed through them.

Problem statement

A two-person shop had no digital presence that matched how it really sells.

Context
Stationery, electrical goods and legal consultancy from one counter in Vadodara.
How it trades
Cash, card swipe and UPI QR at the counter, with stock confirmed over WhatsApp.
Risk
A generic online-store template would promise payment and stock the shop cannot honestly guarantee.

How might we...

Show three trades without three websites?

Let category structure carry the difference instead of separate mini-sites.

Take requests without faking online payment?

End checkout in an honest request that the counter settles.

Use AI without it becoming the price list?

Keep Veronica a client of the same validated services as everything else.

Design principles

Goals and how each was checked

Design goal

Represent every trade

Stationery, Electrical and Legal read clearly from the first screen. Checked by design review against the printed pamphlet.

Design goal

Make the handoff obvious

Cart to request in three routes: /cart, /checkout, /order-success. Checked by walking the flow end to end.

Design goal

Keep the counter fast and safe

Cashiers can bill without admin credentials. Checked through the role and permission model in code.

Design goal

Stay accessible

Skip link, landmarks, contrast and visible focus rings. Checked with automated WCAG AA passes, not yet with assistive-tech users.

03
Research & constraints

The hard requirements came from a cash register, not a survey

No user interviews were run for this project. What shaped it instead were two things every retail software project like this eventually meets: Indian GST law, and the physical reality of a single shop counter.

Framing This chapter documents real constraints from the project's own setup manuals and audit notes. It is not user research, and isn't presented as such.

Problem → cause → design opportunity

Pick a problem.

GST is not optional

Five slabs (0/5/12/18/28%), CGST+SGST for intra-state Gujarat sales, IGST for inter-state. The setup manual includes exact worked tests, e.g. ₹200 at 18% → CGST ₹18 + SGST ₹18 = ₹236.

WhatsApp delivery must be honest

The manual is explicit: record OPENED_IN_WHATSAPP, never claim delivery just because the WhatsApp link opened. Automatic delivery needs a real WhatsApp Business/API provider that wasn't in place.

One SQLite file ≠ one shop

A standalone install has its own local database. The manual explicitly warns against assuming a second counter PC shares the first one's inventory without a real central-server/LAN setup.

Design decision

Treat the POS as the one source of truth

What
The storefront and Veronica both defer to the POS/database for products, prices, tax and stock; the AI model never becomes the record of truth.
Why
Stated as the audit's "Absolute Architectural Law" — money and tax records can't live in a chat model's memory.
Evidence
VERONICA_POS_INTEGRATION_AUDIT.md, section 1.
Alternative considered
Let Veronica quote live prices directly from conversation context.
Trade-off
Slightly more latency and engineering to route everything through validated services.
Validation
Enforced in code (RBAC + service layer); not yet tested with real shop traffic.

05
Information architecture

One sitemap, five real roles

The public site is small on purpose. The complexity lives behind the POS passcode, gated by a role hierarchy that already exists in the code.

Sitemap

Tap an area — these are the actual routes in src/routes/.

Role hierarchy & permissions

Real RBAC from src/server/commerce/rbac.ts: five roles, nine privileged permissions, each gated to a minimum role. Select a role to see what it can do.

Real Cashier accounts are deliberately kept below Manager — the go-live manual repeats "never give cashier staff the Admin credentials" as a standalone rule.

Order state machine

From the integration audit: every order is VX-ORD-2026-XXXXXX, moving through an explicit, logged state machine rather than a single "paid" flag.

06
Brand & moodboard

The brand already existed on paper

Navy and gold, a monogram, a GST receipt layout and a printed pamphlet — the digital product had to sit inside a visual identity that was already printed and laminated, not invent one from scratch.

Tokens pulled from the codebase

These are not proposed colours — they're the exact @theme values in src/styles.css. Click a swatch to copy its hex.

Type

ManropeInter, body & UI

Manrope for display headings, Inter for everything users read and click — the same pairing used across the receipt, the pamphlet's Latin type and the storefront.

Why gold-on-navy

The monogram and both receipt formats were already gold foil on navy blue before the website existed. The site's dark theme, gold CTAs and thin gold borders on figures in this case study are a direct match to that printed identity, not a "premium dark mode" trend choice.

08
High-fidelity screens

The shipped screens

Real production screenshots — the storefront, the checkout, the account area, the deals page and the order-confirmation screen.

Design decision

Checkout ends in a request, not a payment

What
Checkout produces an order request for store pickup or delivery; no card form, no online payment step.
Why
The shop settles in cash, card-swipe at the counter, or store UPI QR — building a fake online payment step would be dishonest to how the business actually runs.
Evidence
PRODUCTION_BASELINE.md, integration boundaries.
Alternative
Integrate a payment gateway immediately.
Trade-off
Conversion happens over WhatsApp/phone, one step slower than a checkout button.
Validation
Matches the shop's real settlement methods; not yet load-tested with real order volume.

09
The AI concierge

Veronica suggests. The POS decides.

The integration audit states this as an "absolute architectural law": the AI model is never the source of truth for products, prices, tax, balances, order state or receipts.

Veronica is a floating chat drawer. She can search the catalogue, calculate GST-inclusive pricing, and prepare a pickup or delivery request with suggested-action chips like Blue Pens, Notebooks & Paper and Build Order Request.

Every one of those actions still passes through the same validated application services and role checks as a human using the storefront — she doesn't get a side door into inventory or payments.

Where she sits in the architecture

10
Testing, GST & go-live

Software passing tests is not the same as a shop being ready

The project's own go-live manual says this outright — twice. Automated tests cover the code; a separate physical checklist covers the shop.

Automated, in the repo

  • 38 automated test cases passing (unit + integration)
  • tsc --noEmit — zero TypeScript errors
  • Production build completes cleanly (~2s, Vercel Nitro)
  • Zero exposed secrets / hardcoded keys
  • WCAG AA pass: skip link, landmarks, contrast, 2px gold focus rings
  • Responsive QA 320–1920px, zero horizontal overflow, 44px touch targets

Physical, at the shop counter

  • Barcode scanner, thermal (58/80mm) and A4 printer tested with real paper
  • A real small UPI payment sent before customer use — never trust the QR image alone
  • WhatsApp receipt: confirm it only opened, never assume delivery
  • Backup restored into a separate database, never over the live one
  • 7-day parallel pilot against the shop's existing method, discrepancies investigated daily

11
Engineering & deployment

What it's actually built and run on

TanStack Start on Vite, deployed to Vercel's Mumbai region — chosen for one concrete reason: it's the closest region to Vadodara.

Frontend

React 19, TanStack Start & Router, Tailwind CSS v4, Radix UI primitives.

Data

@electric-sql/PGlite (Postgres in-process) with a migration runner; no external DB secrets required to deploy.

Hosting

Vercel, Node 22 runtime, region bom1 (Mumbai), 5s max duration, 512MB memory, HSTS + nosniff headers.

Caching, set deliberately per asset type

AssetPolicyWhy
Product photography1 year, immutablePhotos rarely change
Hashed JS/CSS1 year, immutableFingerprinted at build
Icons / OG card1 day + stale-while-revalidateSafe to refresh after a brand update
HTMLRevalidate immediatelyOpen Graph tags are host-specific

Frozen at this baseline

The production baseline formally freezes visual systems, components, routes, data layers and business rules — "no unsolicited feature alterations or cosmetic redesigns."

Known, named limitations

  • Online orders don't decrement hardware POS stock automatically
  • No remote card tokenisation — settlement is in person or by UPI QR
  • Production custom domain awaiting the owner's DNS configuration

12
Outcome & what's next

Honest about what's live, and what isn't yet

The most senior thing about this project may be its known-limitations list — written down before launch, not discovered after.

Shipped

  • Storefront: home, shop, product, cart, checkout, account, deals, wishlist, contact, about
  • POS terminal with role-gated access
  • Veronica AI concierge with suggested-action chips
  • Dual receipt formats (colour + thermal black), GST-correct
  • Deployed on Vercel, Mumbai region

Deliberately not yet connected

  • Live inventory sync between storefront and POS
  • Online payment gateway
  • Automatic WhatsApp PDF delivery (needs a real WhatsApp Business/API provider)
  • Multi-counter shared inventory (needs the central-server/LAN architecture)

What this project reinforced

1 — Say what isn't done

A written "not connected" list did more for trust here than any polish would have.

2 — Let the AI suggest, not decide

Keeping Veronica outside the source of truth kept every legal and financial rule in one place.

3 — Design for the counter, not just the screen

Barcode scanners, thermal paper widths and UPI QR codes are UI surfaces too.

If I had another sprint

Recommended

Counter usability sessions

Five in-store sessions on the request flow, tracking task success and where people reach for a pay button.

Recommended

Measure the WhatsApp handoff

Track the time from request to stock confirmation to learn where the one-step-slower flow costs orders.

Recommended

Assistive-tech pass

Screen reader and keyboard-only sessions on real devices to back up the automated AA checks.

Real First production invoice, opening cash count and the physical go-live sign-off are still tracked on paper in the setup manuals — the software is verified; the shop's own pilot reconciliation is the remaining step before Veronica and the POS become VS Veronixx's sole record.
